seen_animation: Frames 1-6: a line-drawn pig stands in side view facing left, with a spiral snout at the left, two zigzag ears, a rounded body and four short stick legs. It barely changes; the head dips a little lower in frames 5-6. Frame 7: the body shifts slightly right and down and the front legs move apart, as if a step starts. Frame 8: the ears jump from above the snout to the top of the head further right, the head outline becomes a short vertical edge, and the body flattens and widens. Frames 9-10: the body tilts with its back end raised to the upper right and the head lower left, and the ears spread into a wide W. Frames 11-16: the drawing is much larger and fills the frame. The pig is a big tilted wedge with the snout at lower left, the ears near the top left, and short leg strokes along the bottom edge. The head drops to the bottom-left corner in frame 13 and comes back up in frames 14-16. The grey scenery lines shift and change angle from frame 9 on.
seen_film: Frames 1-6: a white pig stands in side view facing left in a concrete pen. Its snout is held up by a catch-pole whose wire loop is around the upper jaw, and a handler's legs are visible behind it. Frame 7: the pole is coming off and the pig begins to move, stepping its front leg forward and starting to turn its head. Frame 8: the pole is gone and the pig's head has turned toward the camera, so both ears and the front of the face are visible. Frames 9-12: the pig walks forward and to the left toward the camera, turned three-quarters, and grows larger in the frame. Frame 13: the camera reframes, and the pig's head sits low at the bottom left with the body filling the upper right. Frames 14-16: the pig is close to the camera in three-quarter front view, its head at left-centre, walking slowly with its face toward the lens.
named_subject: A pig (the doodle in c.png: a pig in side view with a spiral snout, zigzag ears and stick legs).
evidence: The timing and framing match the film. In frames 1-6 of both, the pig stands still in profile. Frame 7 is the first movement in both. In both, frames 11-16 are the close, large framing, with the head dropping to the bottom left in frame 13. What is missing is the event itself. In film frames 1-6 the snout is held by a catch-pole, and in frames 7-8 the pole comes off and the pig turns its face to the camera. The animation draws no pole, so nothing is released. Its snout remains a side-view spiral on the left edge of the head in every frame from 1 to 16; in film frames 8-16 the snout faces the camera. The turn is shown only by the ears moving right and the body tilting, which reads as the pig leaning or shrinking, not as the pig turning toward the viewer. There are also jumps. Between frames 7 and 8 the ears move to a new place on the head and the head outline is redrawn. Between frames 10 and 11 the whole drawing grows to about 1.5 times its size in one step, while the film grows gradually across frames 9-12. Between frames 10 and 11 the grey ground and fence lines also change angle. In frames 11-16 the legs shrink to a few short strokes at the bottom edge, so the walking in film frames 9-16 does not come through. These are still frames only; playback was not seen.
primary_gap: The pig never turns its face toward the camera and the catch-pole release is absent, so the film's event (a held pig is let go, turns, and walks toward the viewer) reads instead as a side-view pig tilting and growing.
closes_when: From frame 8 on, the spiral snout moves from the side edge of the head to the middle of a front-facing head with an ear on each side, and frames 1-6 show a line from the upper left to the snout that is gone by frame 8.
protect: Keep the doodle's construction: the small square-in-circle spiral snout, the two-point zigzag ears, the open outline made of separate straight segments with gaps, the doubled short strokes on the rear, and the stick legs. Keep the still profile in frames 1-6, the first movement at frame 7, the close framing in frames 11-16 with the frame 13 dip, and the sparse grey scenery.
identity_gap: The drawing keeps the doodle's snout, ears and segmented outline, but in frames 11-16 the body becomes a sharp-cornered wedge with the ear stroke separated from the back line, and the legs are reduced to a few strokes, which makes it less round and less complete than c.png.
